title: My family
goal: Name the members of your family, use the possessives nire/zure/haren and the possessive ending -ren, and describe people with adjectives.
bekal: name everyone in your close family and ask about someone else's
use *nire*, *zure*, *haren* and attach *-ren* to people's names
answer *nolakoa da?* with adjectives for people

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Familiaren argazkia
dialogs.intro: A break at the euskaltegi. Budi shows a photo of his family to Maite, a classmate.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bai, hau nire familiaren argazkia da.
lines.id: Yes, this is a photo of my family.
lines.literal: yes, this my family-'s photo-the is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nire aita da. Hirurogei urte ditu.
lines.literal: my father is. sixty year he-has-them.

lines.speaker: Maite:
lines.id: And the woman next to him?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nire ama. Irakaslea da, zu bezala.
lines.id: My mother. She's a teacher, like you.
lines.literal: my mother. teacher-the is, you like.

lines.speaker: Maite:
lines.id: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bai, arreba bat eta anaia bat ditut.
lines.id: Yes, I have a sister and a brother.
lines.literal: yes, sister one and brother one I-have-them.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Arrebak hogei urte ditu, eta anaiak hamazazpi.
lines.id: My sister is twenty, and my brother is seventeen.
lines.literal: sister-doer twenty year has-them, and brother-doer seventeen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ez, ezkongabea naiz. Baina bikotekide bat dut.
lines.id: No, I'm single. But I have a partner.
lines.literal: no, unmarried-the am. but partner one I-have-it.

notes: **The word for a sibling depends on who's speaking.** This is the Basque quirk that surprises beginners most. If a **man** is speaking: *anaia* (brother), *arreba* (sister). If a **woman** is speaking: *neba* (brother), *ahizpa* (sister). So Budi and Maite use different words for exactly the same relationship.

**Anai-arreba: two words joined to mean "siblings".** Basque likes to pair two words to name the whole group: *anai-arrebak* (siblings), *seme-alabak* (children, sons and daughters), *aitona-amonak* (grandparents), *senar-emazteak* (husband and wife). English does something similar with "brothers and sisters" or "mom and dad".

**Baduzu? — the emphatic ba-.** In questions and emphatic positive sentences, the auxiliary *duzu* often takes the prefix *ba-*: *baduzu?* ("do you have?"), *badakit* ("I know"), *badago* ("there is"). The prefix doesn't change the basic meaning; it adds emphasis, like the "do" in "I *do* have".

**-rik: a special ending for questions and negatives.** *Anai-arreba**rik** baduzu?* and *Ez dut anai-arreba**rik**.* When the thing being talked about may not exist — in a question or a negative sentence — Basque uses *-rik* instead of the article *-a*. It corresponds roughly to English "any".

blocks.text: The possessive stands **in front of** the thing owned — one of the few things in Basque that go in front. The noun itself still takes the article: *nire etxe**a***, not *nire etxe*.
For names and other nouns, possession is marked with *-ren* — and the order is the same as English *'s*: **owner first, thing after**.

blocks.title: Two kinds of "of": -ren and -ko
items: *-ren* is for owners that are **alive** or can own things: *Jonen etxea*, *amaren kotxea*.
*-ko* is for **place, material, and description**: *Bilboko kalea* (a street in Bilbao), *euskarazko liburua* (a book in Basque), *goizeko kafea* (morning coffee).
Quick rule: if English would use *'s*, use *-ren*. If English would say "in", "from", or "made of", use *-ko*.
Names ending in a consonant insert *-e-*: *Jon → Jon**en***, *Iker → Iker**ren*** (with a double *r* because the name ends in *r*).

blocks.title: Why siblings have two names
items: Basque names the relationship **from the speaker's point of view**, not just by the sex of the person being talked about. That's why Budi (a man) has an *arreba*, while Maite (a woman) has an *ahizpa* — though both mean "sister".
Memory trick: **a**naia and **a**rreba are used by men; **n**eba and a**h**izpa by women.
If you get it wrong, nobody will be offended — but people will know at once that you're a beginner, because this is one of the most typical features of the language.
The good news: like English, Basque doesn't distinguish older and younger siblings. *Anaia* is a brother, older or younger. If you need to, you can specify *anaia zaharrena* ("the oldest").

blocks.text: *Nolakoa da?* means "what is he/she like?". The answer is an adjective with the article: *Altua da* (he's tall), *Oso jatorra da* (she's very nice).
Adjectives can be strengthened with *oso* ("very") in front, or *-egi* ("too") at the end: *oso altua* (very tall), *altu**egia*** (too tall). To soften, use *samarra*: *altu samarra* (rather tall).

blocks.title: Ready-to-use sentences about family
items: *Zenbat anai-arreba dituzu?* — "How many brothers and sisters do you have?"
*Nire ama Jakartan bizi da.* — "My mother lives in Jakarta."
*Nire aita erretiratuta dago.* — "My father is retired."
*Familia handia dugu.* — "We have a big family."

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right possessive (nire, zure, haren, gure, zuen, haien).
Translate into Basque. Budi (a man) is speaking.
items: My father is sixty years old.
I don't have any brothers or sisters.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: ditut / bat / eta / anaia / arreba / bat

answers: Nire — Zure — Haren — Gure — Zuen — Haien
Jonen — Bilboko — Maiteren — euskarazko — irakaslearen — Donostiako
